payload.title: LEQ: Continuity and Change in Responses to Famine, Disease, and Environmental Stress, c. 1200 to c. 1750

parts.label: A
parts.prompt:
Between c. 1200 and c. 1750, societies across Afro-Eurasia and the Americas faced harvest failures, epidemic disease, floods, droughts, and the cooling of the Little Ice Age. Rulers, religious institutions, and local communities answered these crises with granaries, labor laws, public works, quarantines, charity, new crops, and new medical practices, and sometimes with persecution or coercion.

Evaluate the extent to which state and community responses to famine, disease, and environmental stress changed from c. 1200 to c. 1750. You are not expected to address the entire time period.

In your response you should do the following:
- Respond to the prompt with a historically defensible thesis or claim that establishes a line of reasoning.
- Describe a broader historical context relevant to the prompt.
- Support an argument in response to the prompt using at least two pieces of specific and relevant evidence.
- Use historical reasoning (continuity and change) to frame or structure an argument that addresses the prompt.
- Use evidence to demonstrate a complex understanding of the historical development that is the focus of the prompt.
parts.model_answer:
Between 1200 and 1750, states and communities responded to famine, disease and environmental stress with a mix of old and new methods. Responses changed significantly in that governments after the Black Death began using more organized tools like quarantine, labor laws and new crops from the Columbian Exchange, but there was also strong continuity because states still relied on stored grain and religious explanations, and many responses were really about keeping control of labor and protecting the ruler's legitimacy.

In the 1200s and 1300s the Mongol Empire connected much of Afro-Eurasia through trade routes like the Silk Roads. This made it easier for goods and people to move, but it also helped spread the bubonic plague from Central Asia to the Middle East and Europe in the 1340s. Later the Little Ice Age brought colder weather and bad harvests to many regions, especially in the 1600s. At the same time, bigger empires with bureaucracies, like Ming and Qing China and the Tokugawa shogunate, had more ability to collect and redistribute resources, so they could respond to crises on a larger scale than earlier states.

One change was in how societies dealt with epidemic disease. When the Black Death first hit, many people saw it as punishment from God. Flagellants whipped themselves in public, and in some places Jews were blamed for poisoning wells and were attacked or killed. These responses were religious and based on scapegoating. But some cities began trying more practical methods. In 1377 Ragusa (Dubrovnik) required travelers coming from plague areas to be isolated for 30 days before entering, and later this became the 40 day quarantine used by Venice and other Italian cities. This shows a change toward state-run public health, although religious processions and prayers continued alongside quarantine, so the old response did not disappear.

Labor laws also show how governments responded to crisis in a way that protected the elite. After so many peasants died, workers in England demanded higher wages. The Ordinance of Labourers of 1349 tried to freeze wages at pre-plague levels and force people to work. This was a response to disease, but it was mainly about keeping landowners in control. A similar connection between crisis and labor control happened in the Americas after 1492. Smallpox and other diseases from the Columbian Exchange killed a huge part of the Indigenous population. In the Andes, the Inca had used mit'a labor to fill storehouses that fed people in bad years, but the Spanish turned the mita into forced labor at the silver mines of Potosi, and they resettled surviving Indigenous people into new towns so they were easier to tax and use for labor. So the Spanish kept an older system but changed its purpose from relief to extraction.

Food crises show the most continuity. Chinese dynasties had kept ever-normal granaries for centuries, buying grain when it was cheap and selling it when it was expensive, and the Qing continued this into the 1700s because providing relief supported the idea of the Mandate of Heaven. The Inca storehouses had a similar purpose of making the state look like a provider. What changed was the crops available. After the Kyoho famine in the 1730s, the Tokugawa government promoted sweet potatoes, a crop that originally came from the Americas, because they grew well in poor soil. New World crops like maize and sweet potatoes also spread in China and helped the population grow.

Overall, responses to crisis changed a lot in their methods, as quarantine, American crops and new labor systems appeared, but the goals behind them stayed similar. Rulers wanted to keep order, control workers and show they deserved to rule, which is why granaries and religious responses lasted even as new tools were added.

rubric_rows.criterion: A claim that judges how far responses to famine, disease, or environmental stress changed between c. 1200 and c. 1750, and gives a line of reasoning such as continued reliance on stored grain and religious ritual alongside new quarantine practices, new crops, or colonial labor policies.

Describes a broader setting such as the Mongol-era networks that spread the plague in the 1300s, the cooling and climate instability of the Little Ice Age, the Columbian Exchange after 1492, or the growth of bureaucratic and gunpowder empires that could collect and redistribute resources.

Specific examples of responses, such as the English Ordinance of Labourers of 1349, the 30-day isolation rule at Ragusa in 1377, Inca storehouses supplied through mit'a labor in the Andes, Chinese ever-normal granaries, Tokugawa promotion of sweet potatoes after the Kyoho famine, or Spanish resettlement of Indigenous communities in central Mexico and the Andes after epidemics.

Uses continuity and change to frame the argument, for example by contrasting responses from before and after 1450 or before and after the Columbian Exchange; a complex answer might weigh change against continuity, compare regions, explain why some responses changed while others persisted, or tie state relief to labor control and political legitimacy.

Scoring guide (ALTON reference — not official AP scoring). This question is worth 6 points.
Thesis/claim (0-1): A claim that judges how far responses to famine, disease, or environmental stress changed between c. 1200 and c. 1750, and gives a line of reasoning such as continued reliance on stored grain and religious ritual alongside new quarantine practices, new crops, or colonial labor policies.
   - 1: Makes a defensible claim about the extent of change or continuity in responses to famine, disease, or environmental stress and indicates the reasons or categories that will organize the argument.
   - 0: Gives no defensible claim, simply restates the prompt, or makes a claim that does not address the extent of change or continuity in responses.
Contextualization (0-1): Describes a broader setting such as the Mongol-era networks that spread the plague in the 1300s, the cooling and climate instability of the Little Ice Age, the Columbian Exchange after 1492, or the growth of bureaucratic and gunpowder empires that could collect and redistribute resources.
   - 1: Describes a broader development before, during, or around the period and links it to how states or communities responded to crisis.
   - 0: Offers no relevant context or only a passing phrase not tied to the argument.
Evidence (0-2): Specific examples of responses, such as the English Ordinance of Labourers of 1349, the 30-day isolation rule at Ragusa in 1377, Inca storehouses supplied through mit'a labor in the Andes, Chinese ever-normal granaries, Tokugawa promotion of sweet potatoes after the Kyoho famine, or Spanish resettlement of Indigenous communities in central Mexico and the Andes after epidemics.
   - 2: Uses at least two specific, accurate examples to support an argument about the extent of change or continuity in responses.
   - 1: Identifies at least two specific, accurate examples relevant to responses to famine, disease, or environmental stress.
   - 0: Provides no specific examples, or only vague references to disease or famine.
Analysis and reasoning (0-2): Uses continuity and change to frame the argument, for example by contrasting responses from before and after 1450 or before and after the Columbian Exchange; a complex answer might weigh change against continuity, compare regions, explain why some responses changed while others persisted, or tie state relief to labor control and political legitimacy.
   - 2: Shows a complex understanding, for example by explaining both change and continuity, by analyzing several causes of change, or by making a supported cross-regional comparison or connection.
   - 1: Uses continuity and change to frame or structure an argument about state and community responses.
   - 0: Lists examples without historical reasoning about change or continuity.
Note: Examples may come from any region; an essay need not include the Americas, but American examples must name the specific region and its own labor system, such as the Andean mit'a, the Spanish colonial mita at Potosi, or the encomienda in New Spain.
Note: Persecution, scapegoating, and coercive labor policies count as responses and can support the argument; graders should credit accurate analysis of them without requiring moral judgment.
Note: Claims that one crisis by itself caused the fall of a dynasty or empire should not earn credit as evidence unless the essay qualifies them; coincidence of crisis and rebellion may be described.
Note: The thesis may appear in the introduction or conclusion but must be in one place, not pieced together from scattered sentences.

Sample response, middle score (5/6; Thesis/claim 1, Contextualization 1, Evidence 2, Analysis and reasoning 1):
Between 1200 and 1750 responses to famine, disease, and environmental stress changed somewhat, but many older methods stayed in use. States kept relying on stored grain and on controlling labor, while new ideas like quarantine appeared after the plague. I will show this by looking at responses to the Black Death and then at responses to famine.

The Black Death in the 1300s was a huge crisis that spread along trade routes across Afro-Eurasia, which were connected by the Mongol empire. This killed a very large share of the people in many places and forced governments to react.

One response was in England. In 1349 the English government issued the Ordinance of Labourers. After so many workers died, wages went up because there were fewer peasants to do the work. The ordinance said that workers had to accept the wages that were paid before the plague and could not refuse to work. This was a way for the king and landlords to keep control of labor. Later, in 1351, the Statute of Labourers repeated these rules. So the government answered the disease by making laws about workers instead of helping the sick.

A different response happened in the city of Ragusa on the Adriatic coast. In 1377 Ragusa made a rule that travelers coming from places with plague had to wait thirty days in isolation before entering the city. Later the waiting time grew to forty days, which is where the word quarantine comes from. This was a new way of dealing with disease because it tried to stop the sickness from spreading by separating people.

For famine, states in many places continued to use granaries. In China the government used ever-normal granaries to store grain and sell it cheaply when prices were high. This was something that had been done for a long time before 1200 and kept going afterward. Religious institutions and villages also kept helping the poor with charity and prayer.

In conclusion, there was some change because of quarantine, which was new, but there was also a lot of continuity because granaries and labor control stayed important. The responses of England and Ragusa show that different places did different things, and the Chinese granaries show that old methods lasted. Overall the responses changed a moderate amount from 1200 to 1750.
   - "changed somewhat, but many older methods stayed in use" - Defensible claim about the extent of change and continuity, with categories (plague response, famine response). Earns the thesis point, though the reasoning is basic.
   - "which were connected by the Mongol empire" - Only a brief, one-sentence mention of context (Mongol-connected networks). It is not developed or linked to how states responded, so no contextualization credit.
   - "In 1349 the English government issued the Ordinance of Labourers." - Specific, accurate example described with detail (wage freeze, forced work). Counts toward the two examples needed for the first evidence point.
   - "In 1377 Ragusa made a rule that travelers coming from places with plague had to wait thirty days" - Second specific, accurate example. Both examples are described, but they are not used to argue how much change or continuity there was, so the second evidence point is not earned.
   - "This was a new way of dealing with disease because it tried to stop the sickness from spreading" - Briefly notes something new, but the essay does not compare it to earlier responses or explain why it changed, so this is mostly description.
   - "The responses of England and Ragusa show that different places did different things" - Conclusion restates examples rather than weighing change against continuity or explaining causes. Analysis stays at simple description with no complexity.

Sample response, low score (2/6; Thesis/claim 0, Contextualization 0, Evidence 1, Analysis and reasoning 1):
Between 1200 and 1750 states and communities responded to famine, disease, and environmental stress in many ways. Some things changed and some things stayed the same, so the responses changed to a certain extent but also kept continuity. This essay will look at both change and continuity in how people dealt with these problems.

During this time there were many crises. There was the Black Death in the 1300s and the weather got colder in what is called the Little Ice Age. Many people died and harvests failed in a lot of places, so rulers and communities had to figure out what to do.

One response was storing grain. In China the government used granaries to keep food for bad years, and this kept going for a long time, so it shows continuity. People also turned to religion and charity when things got bad, since they believed God or the gods could help with disease and hunger.

Another response was quarantine. In 1377 the city of Ragusa made ships wait thirty days before people could come ashore because of plague. This was a new idea compared to just praying, so it shows change. Over time more cities copied this kind of thing.

In conclusion, responses to famine and disease changed some because of new ideas like quarantine, but they also stayed the same in other ways like storing grain. Overall there was both change and continuity between 1200 and 1750.
   - "so the responses changed to a certain extent but also kept continuity" - Thesis only restates the prompt's change/continuity question and gives no specific line of reasoning or categories, so it earns no thesis credit.
   - "There was the Black Death in the 1300s and the weather got colder in what is called the Little Ice Age." - Lists crises as a passing mention and does not link them to how states or communities responded, so contextualization earns no credit.
   - "In China the government used granaries to keep food for bad years" - General statement with no specific named institution, date, or detail (such as the ever-normal granary system), so it is too vague to count as specific evidence.
   - "In 1377 the city of Ragusa made ships wait thirty days before people could come ashore because of plague." - This accurate, specific example is the only one in the essay; one example is not enough for evidence credit, which requires at least two.
   - "This was a new idea compared to just praying, so it shows change." - Labels the example as change but does not explain why it changed or what caused it; the essay lists examples without real analysis of continuity and change, so no reasoning credit.

defensible_theses: Responses changed significantly in method after c. 1450 as states adopted quarantine, new American crops, and in some places variolation, but the underlying aims of feeding subjects to preserve order and blaming or controlling vulnerable groups continued from the Black Death era.

Continuity outweighed change: from the Song-Yuan-Ming granary tradition to Inca storehouses to Tokugawa relief, states relied mostly on stored food, labor mobilization, and religious ritual, while truly new practices such as lazarettos and the spread of sweet potatoes added to these tools rather than replacing them.

Responses changed most in the Americas, where Spanish colonizers answered epidemic population collapse with resettlement and coercive labor drafts that replaced Andean and Mesoamerican systems of reciprocal redistribution, while Afro-Eurasian states mostly expanded older relief practices.
contextualization_ideas: Mongol-era trade and military networks across Eurasia in the 1200s and 1300s helped carry the plague that became the Black Death in the 1340s, shaping the first great wave of responses.
Climate cooling and instability associated with the Little Ice Age brought harvest failures in many regions during the 1600s, a time often called the seventeenth-century crisis.

The Columbian Exchange after 1492 spread Afro-Eurasian diseases to the Americas and American crops such as maize, potatoes, and sweet potatoes to Afro-Eurasia, changing both the crises and the tools for answering them.
outside_evidence: England's Ordinance of Labourers (1349) and Statute of Labourers (1351) tried to fix wages at pre-plague levels after the Black Death caused labor shortages.
Ragusa (Dubrovnik) required a 30-day isolation of arrivals in 1377, and Venice set up a permanent lazaretto in 1423, early institutional quarantine measures.

During the Black Death, Jewish communities in many European towns, including Strasbourg in 1349, were attacked after false accusations of causing the plague, while flagellant movements staged public penance.
The Great Famine of 1315 to 1317 in northern Europe brought widespread starvation after repeated harvest failures.
Chinese dynasties maintained ever-normal granaries to buy grain in good years and sell or distribute it in bad years; the Qing expanded this granary system in the 1700s.
Sweet potatoes and maize from the Americas spread in China during the 1600s and 1700s and helped farmers cultivate hilly land and support population growth.
In the Andes, the Inca state used mit'a rotational labor to build roads and terraces and to fill qollqa storehouses that held food for times of shortage.

After smallpox struck Tenochtitlan in 1520 and later epidemics reduced Indigenous populations in central Mexico, Spanish authorities consolidated surviving communities into congregaciones, or reducciones, for labor, tribute, and conversion.
In the 1570s Viceroy Francisco de Toledo reorganized the mita in the Andes into a colonial labor draft that sent Indigenous workers to the Potosi silver mines.
The Spanish Crown's New Laws of 1542 sought to limit encomienda abuses amid the decline of Indigenous populations.
Tokugawa Yoshimune's government promoted sweet potato cultivation, associated with the scholar Aoki Kon'yo, after the Kyoho famine of 1732 to 1733.
The Mamluk sultan Qalawun founded a large hospital in Cairo in the 1280s, an example of charitable medical institutions in the Islamic world, often supported through waqf endowments.
Variolation, deliberate exposure to smallpox material, was practiced in China and the Ottoman Empire; Lady Mary Wortley Montagu observed it in Istanbul and promoted it in England around 1721.
England's Poor Law of 1601 made parishes responsible for relief of the poor through local taxes.
reasoning_types: Causation (why some responses shifted, such as new crops after the Columbian Exchange)
Comparison across regions as a complexity move
common_pitfalls: Describing the crises themselves (plague deaths, famine) without discussing how states or communities responded.
Treating the Black Death or the Little Ice Age as the single cause of a dynasty's fall rather than one factor among several.
Writing only about Europe, or only listing examples without a judgment on the extent of change.
Using vague phrases like 'Native Americans were forced to work' instead of naming the region and labor system, such as the Andean mit'a or the Potosi mita.
Confusing the pre-colonial Inca mit'a, built on reciprocity and state redistribution, with the colonial Spanish mita at Potosi.
Moving well past 1750 to examples such as Jenner's vaccine of 1796 without tying them back to the period.
facts: The Black Death spread through Afro-Eurasia from the 1340s, reaching Europe and the Mediterranean in 1347 to 1351.
England issued the Ordinance of Labourers in 1349 and the Statute of Labourers in 1351.
Ragusa adopted a 30-day isolation rule in 1377; the word quarantine comes from the later 40-day period.
The New Laws were issued in 1542.
Francisco de Toledo was viceroy of Peru in the 1570s and organized the Potosi mita.
The Kyoho famine occurred in 1732 to 1733 under Tokugawa Yoshimune.
England's Poor Law was enacted in 1601.

annotations.comment: Complexity: weighs continuity against change and makes a cross-regional link between Andean and Spanish labor systems.

annotations.quote: because providing relief supported the idea of the Mandate of Heaven
annotations.comment: Explains why some responses lasted by tying them to legitimacy. The ideas are strong, but the China and Japan evidence is brief, which keeps this from being a top essay.

samples.essay:
Between 1200 and 1750 responses to famine, disease, and environmental stress changed somewhat, but many older methods stayed in use. States kept relying on stored grain and on controlling labor, while new ideas like quarantine appeared after the plague. I will show this by looking at responses to the Black Death and then at responses to famine.

The Black Death in the 1300s was a huge crisis that spread along trade routes across Afro-Eurasia, which were connected by the Mongol empire. This killed a very large share of the people in many places and forced governments to react.

One response was in England. In 1349 the English government issued the Ordinance of Labourers. After so many workers died, wages went up because there were fewer peasants to do the work. The ordinance said that workers had to accept the wages that were paid before the plague and could not refuse to work. This was a way for the king and landlords to keep control of labor. Later, in 1351, the Statute of Labourers repeated these rules. So the government answered the disease by making laws about workers instead of helping the sick.

A different response happened in the city of Ragusa on the Adriatic coast. In 1377 Ragusa made a rule that travelers coming from places with plague had to wait thirty days in isolation before entering the city. Later the waiting time grew to forty days, which is where the word quarantine comes from. This was a new way of dealing with disease because it tried to stop the sickness from spreading by separating people.

For famine, states in many places continued to use granaries. In China the government used ever-normal granaries to store grain and sell it cheaply when prices were high. This was something that had been done for a long time before 1200 and kept going afterward. Religious institutions and villages also kept helping the poor with charity and prayer.

In conclusion, there was some change because of quarantine, which was new, but there was also a lot of continuity because granaries and labor control stayed important. The responses of England and Ragusa show that different places did different things, and the Chinese granaries show that old methods lasted. Overall the responses changed a moderate amount from 1200 to 1750.

annotations.quote: changed somewhat, but many older methods stayed in use
annotations.comment: Defensible claim about the extent of change and continuity, with categories (plague response, famine response). Earns the thesis point, though the reasoning is basic.

annotations.quote: which were connected by the Mongol empire
annotations.comment: Only a brief, one-sentence mention of context (Mongol-connected networks). It is not developed or linked to how states responded, so no contextualization credit.

annotations.quote: In 1349 the English government issued the Ordinance of Labourers.
annotations.comment: Specific, accurate example described with detail (wage freeze, forced work). Counts toward the two examples needed for the first evidence point.

annotations.quote: In 1377 Ragusa made a rule that travelers coming from places with plague had to wait thirty days
annotations.comment: Second specific, accurate example. Both examples are described, but they are not used to argue how much change or continuity there was, so the second evidence point is not earned.

annotations.quote: This was a new way of dealing with disease because it tried to stop the sickness from spreading
annotations.comment: Briefly notes something new, but the essay does not compare it to earlier responses or explain why it changed, so this is mostly description.

annotations.quote: The responses of England and Ragusa show that different places did different things
annotations.comment: Conclusion restates examples rather than weighing change against continuity or explaining causes. Analysis stays at simple description with no complexity.

samples.essay:
Between 1200 and 1750 states and communities responded to famine, disease, and environmental stress in many ways. Some things changed and some things stayed the same, so the responses changed to a certain extent but also kept continuity. This essay will look at both change and continuity in how people dealt with these problems.

During this time there were many crises. There was the Black Death in the 1300s and the weather got colder in what is called the Little Ice Age. Many people died and harvests failed in a lot of places, so rulers and communities had to figure out what to do.

One response was storing grain. In China the government used granaries to keep food for bad years, and this kept going for a long time, so it shows continuity. People also turned to religion and charity when things got bad, since they believed God or the gods could help with disease and hunger.

Another response was quarantine. In 1377 the city of Ragusa made ships wait thirty days before people could come ashore because of plague. This was a new idea compared to just praying, so it shows change. Over time more cities copied this kind of thing.

In conclusion, responses to famine and disease changed some because of new ideas like quarantine, but they also stayed the same in other ways like storing grain. Overall there was both change and continuity between 1200 and 1750.

annotations.quote: so the responses changed to a certain extent but also kept continuity
annotations.comment: Thesis only restates the prompt's change/continuity question and gives no specific line of reasoning or categories, so it earns no thesis credit.

annotations.quote: There was the Black Death in the 1300s and the weather got colder in what is called the Little Ice Age.
annotations.comment: Lists crises as a passing mention and does not link them to how states or communities responded, so contextualization earns no credit.

annotations.quote: In China the government used granaries to keep food for bad years
annotations.comment: General statement with no specific named institution, date, or detail (such as the ever-normal granary system), so it is too vague to count as specific evidence.

annotations.quote: In 1377 the city of Ragusa made ships wait thirty days before people could come ashore because of plague.
annotations.comment: This accurate, specific example is the only one in the essay; one example is not enough for evidence credit, which requires at least two.

annotations.quote: This was a new idea compared to just praying, so it shows change.
annotations.comment: Labels the example as change but does not explain why it changed or what caused it; the essay lists examples without real analysis of continuity and change, so no reasoning credit.
